text: It’s Marilla. The question says watch how one small mistake turns into a big embarrassment. Well, I’ve watched a good many of Anne’s. This one happens in my own kitchen, with the minister at my table, so you can imagine I have opinions. First there are two word parts that point a direction, and some doing words that tell you when. Then the chapter. Mind the bottles.

The box says a place decides how big a mistake feels. I’ll tell you why that’s so in Avonlea. Everybody knows everybody, and nothing stays in a kitchen. Rachel Lynde will have heard before the dishes are dry. So as you read, ask who’s close enough to see, and who’ll hear about it after. Then ask whether the same mistake would matter in a town where nobody knew your name.

The top sentence is a plain one, and it’s correct. Look at what makes it so. The names start with capitals, the doing word tells you it’s already done, and it stops where it should. The bottom one is about me and my vanilla, and it runs two thoughts together without a breath. Find where one stops and the next starts. Then give my name its capital. I’d thank you to.

Four boxes of word work, and I’ll not pretend they’re exciting. But a girl who can’t tell what’s done from what’s coming is a girl who mixes up her bottles. Two of these are sorting. Put each card where it belongs, then name the groups yourself. Nobody’s going to name them for you. One is typing in a missing piece. Look before you type. I never saw the good of guessing.

Two word parts this week, and each one points a direction. One means against, like a thing that pushes back. The other means away, or down, like leaving the house, or going down the cellar stairs. Read the four words in the box, cover the front, and see what’s left. Then ask which way the front is pushing. Against, or away and down. That’s all there is to it.

Four words, and one of them I’d never say myself. Vivacious. Anne would, and often. Read the sentence above each card before you flip it, the way the box shows you with the first. The words around it will tell you more than you think. Two of those sentences are about Mrs. Allan, and you’ll meet her today. I think well of her. Guess first, then flip. Not the other way round.

Anne baked a cake. Anne bakes a cake. Anne will bake a cake. Same girl, same cake, and I’d wager she does all three before the week is out. What changes is when. Sort the cards by when, then give each group a name of your own. Don’t wait for mine, I haven’t given you any. And say them out loud. Your ear knows more grammar than you think.

Six words, and every one ended in a y before something got added. Sometimes the y stayed put and sometimes it turned into an i. That isn’t whim. Look at the letter sitting just in front of the y, and then look at what got added after it. Sort them by what happened, then name your three groups. A rule you work out yourself sticks better than one I hand you.

One sentence from the start of this chapter, the day the schoolmaster left. I never thought him worth two handkerchiefs, but there it is. Now say it three ways. Change the doing word first. Then start the sentence somewhere else, with a when or a where. Then tell how. Anne could do this in her sleep, and frequently does. You’ll do it awake.

There’s a box here about being seen. I’ll be honest, I didn’t hold with that kind of talk once. A child was fed and clothed and that was that. But there’s a new minister’s wife in Avonlea, and Anne has fallen for her entirely. Watch how Mrs. Allan looks at Anne. Not at what Anne does. At Anne. Then watch whether I do the same. I’m not saying I will.

Two stops, and the first one comes when the cake goes wrong. Read slowly up to the tea. Count who’s at the table, and who’d tell whom. When you reach the stop, think about what Mrs. Allan does, not only what she says. Then read on to the end and listen to what Anne says to me after. I had an answer for her. You can decide whether it was a fair one.

Well. You’ve read it now, so I needn’t tell you what was in that bottle, or whose fault it was. I said partly mine, and I stand by partly. Now you write. Put things in the order they happened. Use the book, not your memory of it. And when you get to Mrs. Allan, use her own words. They’re better than mine, and I’m not too proud to say so.

Three questions. The first is about the bottle and how it got where it was. The hint points at me, and I won’t argue. The second is about why Anne couldn’t smell it. She told me, through a good deal of crying. Find what she said. The third is about Mrs. Allan coming up the stairs. Look for the small thing she asks to see. It tells you more than a speech would.

Your word-parts answer is saved from before. Look at it again now that you’ve read the chapter. Anne went up those stairs as fast as anyone ever has, and Mrs. Allan came up them after her. Ask whether your sentence points a direction, the way those stairs do. Against, or away, or down. If it could belong in this chapter, good. If it couldn’t, think how it might.

Anne’s cake is a story you can only tell in order. The bottle first, then the guests, then the first bite. Tell it backwards and nobody laughs. Today you’re giving the middle of your own story its order. Three scenes, and each one starts with a word that says when. First, then, after that. Pick the ones that fit, not the fanciest. I’d take plain and right over fancy and wrong any day.
